reasons.why: A star within one TESS pixel could cause this dip with an eclipse of 25% or less, and the location measurement does not rule it out. The closest suspect needs an eclipse_needed of 0.1315 and lies 2.5 sigma_from_centroid, so resolved follow-up photometry watching the target and neighbour separately during a dip could settle which star dims.
The dip is not shown to be off_target, but it is also not uniquely on_target, so the neighbours check decides and it raises the flag above.
Odd and even dips match, within the planet-like range.
No convincing second dip elsewhere in the orbit; this low value is treated as noise.
The depth is steady enough across sectors.
The inferred size is in the planet-like range.
The dip lasts about as long as expected for a central crossing.
No known match at this period or a harmonic.
The shape does not favour a V over a flat bottom.
No large swing outside the dip that would suggest rotation or a contact binary.

open_questions: Do any of the fainter stars included in neighbours.could_cause (55 within radius_arcsec 150), but not in plausible_within_1px, need checking for very deep eclipses over 25%? They are not the reason for this flag.
Could data from upcoming sectors 116 and 134 improve the difference-image location enough to separate the target from the nearby suspect?
dossier.public_summary: This star shows a regular, planet-sized dip that passes the other checks, but the view is too blurry to tell it apart from a nearby star that could be eclipsing instead. A sharper follow-up look at the two stars separately is needed before it can move forward.
